recurring_scale_anchors: Canvas 304×192; distinguish movie screens, live stages and auditorium spaces through clear silhouettes.
No readable titles, captions, signage, logos, brands, letters or numerals; use abstract image marks and blank bars only.
Genre cards must show a recognizable cinematic or theatrical situation, while keeping each genre visually distinct.
Keep people and performance gestures large enough to read at the card size; use muted audience and venue details as context.
When dictionary glosses conflict with this chapter group, draw the movie, theater or performance sense shown by its siblings.

polysemy_resolution_table.action movie: A film genre with a protagonist in a dynamic chase or physical rescue shown within a cinema frame; this is the movie type, not a real-life action.
polysemy_resolution_table.ballet: A classical ballet performance with a dancer en pointe, a tutu and a stage; distinguish from generic dance.
polysemy_resolution_table.cartoon: An animated film or show with a drawn character visibly inside a screen; follow the movies-and-shows group rather than political cartoons or mural sketches.
polysemy_resolution_table.comedy: A comic stage or screen performance with an unmistakable harmless physical gag and amused audience; avoid a simple portrait of a smiling person.
polysemy_resolution_table.crime drama: A fictional detective or investigator studying a clue in a dramatic film scene; this is an entertainment genre, not an actual crime scene.
polysemy_resolution_table.drama: A serious theatrical scene with actors in a tense emotional exchange; the Japanese gloss supports a play or dramatic literature, not a life event.
polysemy_resolution_table.horror: A suspenseful fictional screen scene with an eerie shadow or masked figure; keep it non-graphic and clearly entertainment.
polysemy_resolution_table.movie / film: A cinematic story playing on a large screen with viewers and film imagery; the film itself should be central, not the building.
polysemy_resolution_table.musical: A stage production that combines acting, singing and dancing, with a singer and small ensemble; distinct from opera and ballet.
polysemy_resolution_table.opera: A theatrical opera singer in a dramatic costume with curtains and orchestral context; follow the genre group despite the broad alternate gloss.
polysemy_resolution_table.plays (performance): Actors performing a scripted play on a stage before an audience; use the performance noun, not the verb meaning to play.
polysemy_resolution_table.romantic comedy: A lighthearted romantic scene with two characters and a comic mishap or shared laugh; distinguish the blended genre from serious drama.
polysemy_resolution_table.science fiction: A speculative screen story with spacecraft or futuristic technology visible inside a movie frame; not a book cover or real laboratory.
polysemy_resolution_table.shows: Live entertainment or screen productions presented to an audience; use a broad stage/show scene without making it a specific musical or film genre.
polysemy_resolution_table.thriller: A suspenseful fictional situation with a character noticing a looming threat; no supernatural monster, to distinguish it from horror.
polysemy_resolution_table.tragedy: A serious stage story ending in loss, shown through mournful actors and a fallen crown or dimmed stage; avoid depicting real injury.
polysemy_resolution_table.audience: Several spectators facing a performance or screen; make the viewers the focal group, not the performers.
polysemy_resolution_table.cast: The ensemble of actors who appear in a production, grouped together in costume onstage; not an object being thrown.
polysemy_resolution_table.director: A film or theater director guiding performers beside a camera or stage monitor; not a corporate board or general guide.
polysemy_resolution_table.hero: The brave central protagonist visibly helping another character or facing a challenge; distinguish from any famous actor.
polysemy_resolution_table.main character: The central fictional character singled out within a framed story scene while supporting figures remain secondary.
polysemy_resolution_table.movie star / film star: A famous screen actor arriving at a premiere with photographers and camera flashes; keep fame cues separate from ordinary acting.
polysemy_resolution_table.usher: A theater employee guiding a ticket holder to a seat with a small flashlight; not a doorman at a home.
polysemy_resolution_table.villain: The fictional antagonist shown opposing a hero with a guarded, shadowed pose; keep the character safe and non-violent.
polysemy_resolution_table.actor: One performer in costume taking a stage bow; the person is acting, not being shown as a celebrity.
polysemy_resolution_table.character: A fictional person represented within a story frame or script illustration, distinct from a real actor and from personality.
polysemy_resolution_table.balcony (theater): The raised upper seating gallery inside a theater, with rail and seats overlooking the stage; not a home balcony.
polysemy_resolution_table.box office: A staffed theater ticket booth with a customer purchasing admission; no readable signage.
polysemy_resolution_table.movie theater / cinema (also used in the: A public cinema building with several patrons entering toward a screen or auditorium; not home viewing.
polysemy_resolution_table.circle: The curved upper tier of seats inside a theater, viewed as a continuous gallery around the stage; distinct from the projecting balcony and ground-floor stalls.
polysemy_resolution_table.multiplex: A cinema with several separate auditoriums or screening doors shown together; distinguish from a single-screen theater.
polysemy_resolution_table.opera house: A grand performing-arts venue with formal columns, a central entrance and stage curtains; distinguish from a movie cinema.
polysemy_resolution_table.orchestra pit: A recessed space in front of the stage containing seated musicians; show the lowered pit edge clearly.
polysemy_resolution_table.orchestra seating: The main-floor seats nearest the stage, viewed from behind the rows; distinct from the musicians’ orchestra pit.
polysemy_resolution_table.stalls: The ground-floor theater seating section at audience level; use a clear floor-level view and no animal stalls.
polysemy_resolution_table.theater: A live-performance venue with a raised stage, proscenium and audience seating; broad theater sense rather than a movie theater.
polysemy_resolution_table.showtime: The moment a performance or film is about to begin, with a clock and patrons facing an illuminated screen or stage; no clock numerals.
polysemy_resolution_table.ticket: A perforated admission ticket being checked at a theater entrance; avoid transit gates or fares.
polysemy_resolution_table.applause: Spectators clapping while seated after a performance; use repeated hand gestures and small sound arcs.
polysemy_resolution_table.encore: A performer returning to the stage for another bow after applause; show the welcoming crowd and repeated bow gesture.
polysemy_resolution_table.performance: A live entertainer performing onstage before spectators; use a clear peak gesture and visible audience.
polysemy_resolution_table.standing ovation: The audience has risen to its feet and is clapping; distinguish it from seated applause.
polysemy_resolution_table.costumes: Several theatrical costumes on a rail or worn by actors, with distinctive fabric, hats and capes; not ordinary clothing.
polysemy_resolution_table.curtain: A large theater curtain framing an empty stage, with gathered fabric and a central opening; not a home window curtain.
polysemy_resolution_table.dialog / dialogue: Two actors speaking and responding to one another onstage, shown through facing gestures and sound arcs without words.
polysemy_resolution_table.popcorn: A paper tub filled with popped corn beside a few kernels; follow the cinema snack sense.
polysemy_resolution_table.program: A small blank theater program booklet held by an audience member before a performance; distinct from a script.
polysemy_resolution_table.props: Handheld stage objects arranged on a backstage table for actors to use, such as a fan, cane and toy sword; not scenery.
polysemy_resolution_table.screen: A broad, flat projection surface displaying a scene, with projector beam or theater framing; not a wire-mesh window or television set.
polysemy_resolution_table.script: An open actor’s script with blank line marks, page tabs and pencil annotations; no readable writing and no booklet cover image.
polysemy_resolution_table.sets: Stage scenery flats and a constructed backdrop being positioned by stagehands; distinguish physical scenery from handheld props.
polysemy_resolution_table.special effects: A film set using light, fog and a miniature or projected effect to create an impossible image; keep effects visibly produced for a camera.
polysemy_resolution_table.stage: The raised performance platform with wings and proscenium, shown empty so it is not mistaken for a particular show.
polysemy_resolution_table.stunt: A performer safely leaping or swinging for a camera crew, with a mat or harness cue; a performed action, not the film genre.
polysemy_resolution_table.plot: The linked sequence of story events in a production, represented by a storyboard of connected dramatic moments; not a parcel of land.
polysemy_resolution_table.scene: One single framed moment or setting from a production, with actors frozen in place; distinct from the whole plot sequence.
polysemy_resolution_table.subtitles: A film image with two blank caption bars along its lower edge; no letters, words or numerals.

glossary_context_notes: The course group context resolves several inaccurate or broad Japanese glosses: cast means an ensemble of actors; director means a film/theater director; character means a fictional person; circle and stalls are theater seating; screen is a movie projection screen; stunt is a performed movie action; plot is a story sequence; script is a film/play script.

Keep neighboring concepts separate: film vs. cinema building; play/production vs. drama genre; actor vs. movie star; hero vs. main character vs. villain; movie theater vs. opera house; balcony/circle vs. orchestra seating/stalls vs. orchestra pit; stage scenery vs. props; program vs. script; plot vs. one scene; applause vs. standing ovation.
